ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Preregistration: All studies received IRB approval and were preregistered prior to data collection (As predicted #208612).
To measure participants' attitudes toward legal immigrants before the conversation with GPT, we recruited a sample of monolingual English speakers from the UK on Prolific.
In it, participants were instructed to have a conversation with GPT-o1-mini, OpenAI's conversational chatbot.
After the conversation, participants were asked how convincing and pleasant they found the exchange, using a 1-7 Likert scale.
Lastly, participants answered several demographic questions and were debriefed.
A total of 124 participants completed the main study (T2).
In total, 1,448 participants completed the prescreening protocol (T1).
Following preregistered exclusion criteria, eight participants were excluded due to technical issues, and seven additional participants did not complete the survey consecutively.
Four participants indicated that their data should not be used, and three participants took more than 3 SD above the mean completion time (M completion time = 16.17 minutes, SD = 6.54 minutes).
Two additional participants were excluded because they provided an ID that did not match the first wave for a total of 189 participants.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> To measure participants' attitudes toward legal immigrants before the conversation with GPT, we recruited a sample of monolingual English speakers from the UK on Prolific.

> In it, participants were instructed to have a conversation with GPT-o1-mini, OpenAI's conversational chatbot.

> After the conversation, participants were asked how convincing and pleasant they found the exchange, using a 1-7 Likert scale.

> Lastly, participants answered several demographic questions and were debriefed.

> A total of 124 participants completed the main study (T2).

> In total, 1,448 participants completed the prescreening protocol (T1).

> Following preregistered exclusion criteria, eight participants were excluded due to technical issues, and seven additional participants did not complete the survey consecutively.

> Four participants indicated that their data should not be used, and three participants took more than 3 SD above the mean completion time (M completion time = 16.17 minutes, SD = 6.54 minutes).

> Two additional participants were excluded because they provided an ID that did not match the first wave for a total of 189 participants.

Ethics approval statement:

> Preregistration: All studies received IRB approval and were preregistered prior to data collection (As predicted #208612).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

found that the attitudes toward legal immigrants at T1 were a significant positive predictor of the attitudes at T2 (b = .50, SE = 0.22, t = 2.34, p = .02), suggesting that this attitude is generally stable.

Trust in GPT at T1 was a significant negative predictor (b = -1.22, SE = 0.57, t = -2.15, p = .034), indicating that higher initial trust in GPT was associated with less positive attitudes toward immigrants after the conversation with GPT while holding intellectual humility at zero.
Intellectual humility at T2 was not a significant predictor (p = .30) when trust was at zero.

table.formatted: Crucially, there was a significant interaction between trust at T1 and intellectual humility at T2 (b = .35, SE = 0.14, t = 2.42, p = .017), such that participants who were both higher in trust and higher in intellectual humility expressed more positive opinions of legal immigrants after exposure to counter-attitudinal claims, while holding constant their initial attitude toward legal immigrants (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

A simple slope analysis showed that at mean levels of trust, intellectual humility significantly predicted more positive attitudes at T2 (b = .8, SE = 0.27, p = .004).

When examining the main effects, intellectual humility (b = -0.21, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.39], p = .49) and trust in GPT (b = -0.45, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [-1.13, 0.24], p = .20) were not significant predictors individually.

When examining the main effects, intellectual humility (b = -0.21, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.39], p = .49) and trust in GPT (b = -0.45, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [-1.13, 0.24], p = .20) were not significant predictors individually.

The preregistered interaction between intellectual humility and trust in GPT was in the same direction as observed in Study 1 but was not significant (b = 0.11, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.25], p = .09), likely reflecting insufficient statistical power.

Examining the simple slopes for participants with high levels (+1SD from the mean) of trust, there was a positive and significant relationship between intellectual humility and attitude change (b = 0.45, SE = 0.15, p = .004).

In contrast, for those with low levels of trust (-1SD from the mean), this relationship disappeared (b = 0.10, SE = 0.15, p = .52), suggesting that even when a participant is intellectually humble, they do not change their attitudes if they do not trust the source, emphasizing the centrality of both factors.

Regarding the predictors of interest, intellectual humility at T1 did not predict attitudes at T2 when trust was at zero (b = -0.34, SE = 0.28, 95% CI [-0.89, 0.21], p = .22).

Trust in GPT at T1 negatively predicted attitudes at T2 when intellectual humility was at zero (b = -0.65, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-1.26, -0.04], p = .038), but not at mean levels of intellectual humility (b = 0.09, SE = 0.07, p = .22).

Trust in GPT at T1 negatively predicted attitudes at T2 when intellectual humility was at zero (b = -0.65, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-1.26, -0.04], p = .038), but not at mean levels of intellectual humility (b = 0.09, SE = 0.07, p = .22).

Importantly, the preregistered interaction between intellectual humility and trust in GPT at T1 significantly predicted attitudes at T2 (b = 0.14, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.26], p = .016), consistent with the pattern observed in Study 1.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 13 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: There was no significant difference in initial trust in GPT between those with a positive (M = 4.05, SD = 1.26) compared to a negative (M = 4.01, SD = 1.39) opinion about legal immigrants (p = .650) nor in distrust (M pro immigrants = 3.34, SD = 1.38, M anti immigrants = 3.46, SD = 1.42, p = .248).

There was no significant difference in initial trust in GPT between those with a positive (M = 4.05, SD = 1.26) compared to a negative (M = 4.01, SD = 1.39) opinion about legal immigrants (p = .650) nor in distrust (M pro immigrants = 3.34, SD = 1.38, M anti immigrants = 3.46, SD = 1.42, p = .248).
Intellectual humility at T2 was not a significant predictor (p = .30) when trust was at zero.
There were no significant differences in distrust (p = .10).

When examining the main effects, intellectual humility (b = -0.21, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.39], p = .49) and trust in GPT (b = -0.45, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [-1.13, 0.24], p = .20) were not significant predictors individually.

When examining the main effects, intellectual humility (b = -0.21, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.39], p = .49) and trust in GPT (b = -0.45, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [-1.13, 0.24], p = .20) were not significant predictors individually.

The preregistered interaction between intellectual humility and trust in GPT was in the same direction as observed in Study 1 but was not significant (b = 0.11, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.25], p = .09), likely reflecting insufficient statistical power.

In contrast, for those with low levels of trust (-1SD from the mean), this relationship disappeared (b = 0.10, SE = 0.15, p = .52), suggesting that even when a participant is intellectually humble, they do not change their attitudes if they do not trust the source, emphasizing the centrality of both factors.
There was no significant effect of time on intellectual humility, χ²(2) = 0.8, p = .67.

table.formatted: Pairwise contrasts confirmed that intellectual humility did not differ between any two time points (T1: M = 5.09, SD = 1.01; T2: M = 5.11, SD = 1.30; T3: M = 5.15, SD = 1.21; all pairwise ps > .66), indicating that intellectual humility remained stable throughout the study.

Regarding the predictors of interest, intellectual humility at T1 did not predict attitudes at T2 when trust was at zero (b = -0.34, SE = 0.28, 95% CI [-0.89, 0.21], p = .22).

Trust in GPT at T1 negatively predicted attitudes at T2 when intellectual humility was at zero (b = -0.65, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-1.26, -0.04], p = .038), but not at mean levels of intellectual humility (b = 0.09, SE = 0.07, p = .22).

table.formatted: Over time, attitudes at T2 strongly predicted attitudes at T3 (b = 0.64, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.53, 0.75], p < .001), while intellectual humility at T2 did not predict later attitudes (b = 0.04, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.20], p = .57).

stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 2 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: The mean opinion about legal immigrants at the first measurement was 2.23 (SD = 0.79), but after the conversation with GPT, it significantly increased to 3.82 (SD = 1.84), t(104) = -8.89, p < .001 (Figure 1).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: We then fit a linear model predicting participants' opinions at the second measurement from initial trust in GPT 2 and intellectual humility (measured after the conversation), while holding their initial opinion toward immigrants constant (F(4, 100) = 5.312, p < .001, R² = .175, adjusted R² = .142).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: found that the attitudes toward legal immigrants at T1 were a significant positive predictor of the attitudes at T2 (b = .50, SE = 0.22, t = 2.34, p = .02), suggesting that this attitude is generally stable.

Trust in GPT at T1 was a significant negative predictor (b = -1.22, SE = 0.57, t = -2.15, p = .034), indicating that higher initial trust in GPT was associated with less positive attitudes toward immigrants after the conversation with GPT while holding intellectual humility at zero.

Crucially, there was a significant interaction between trust at T1 and intellectual humility at T2 (b = .35, SE = 0.14, t = 2.42, p = .017), such that participants who were both higher in trust and higher in intellectual humility expressed more positive opinions of legal immigrants after exposure to counter-attitudinal claims, while holding constant their initial attitude toward legal immigrants (Figure 2).

At baseline, participants with positive attitudes toward legal immigrants reported higher trust in GPT (M = 4.35, SD = 1.26) compared to those with negative attitudes (M = 4.15, SD = 1.39), t(1047.5) = 2.72, p = .007, 95% CI [0.06, 0.34], d = 0.15.
table.d_coherence_note: Non-integer df indicates Welch's t-test (unequal variances); sample sizes cannot be determined.

table.text: Participants with positive attitudes were, however, more intellectually humble (M = 5.37, SD = 0.87) than those with negative attitudes (M = 5.11, SD = 0.99), t(1446) = 5.15, p < .001, 95% CI [0.16, 0.35], d = 0.28.
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 724, N = 1448).

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 413 columns across 7 data files.
#### Issues Identified

125 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

105 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **76 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Preregistration: All studies received IRB approval and were preregistered prior to data collection (As predicted #208612).
live_data_statements: To measure participants' attitudes toward legal immigrants before the conversation with GPT, we recruited a sample of monolingual English speakers from the UK on Prolific.
In it, participants were instructed to have a conversation with GPT-o1-mini, OpenAI's conversational chatbot.
After the conversation, participants were asked how convincing and pleasant they found the exchange, using a 1-7 Likert scale.
Lastly, participants answered several demographic questions and were debriefed.
A total of 124 participants completed the main study (T2).
In total, 1,448 participants completed the prescreening protocol (T1).
Following preregistered exclusion criteria, eight participants were excluded due to technical issues, and seven additional participants did not complete the survey consecutively.
Four participants indicated that their data should not be used, and three participants took more than 3 SD above the mean completion time (M completion time = 16.17 minutes, SD = 6.54 minutes).
Two additional participants were excluded because they provided an ID that did not match the first wave for a total of 189 participants.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 0 ran without error, 6 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **3 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `Main_Analysis.Rmd` (s1_t1_anonymized.csv, s2_t1_anonymized.csv); `SOM_Analysis.R` (s1_t1_anonymized.csv); `SOM_Analysis.Rmd` (s1_t1_anonymized.csv). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **A script looked for 3 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running it once more we copied them there: `Study 1/s1_t1_anonymized.csv` to `osfstorage-archive/Study 1/Study 1/s1_t1_anonymized.csv` for `Main_Analysis.R`; `Study 1/s1_t2_anonymized.csv` to `osfstorage-archive/Study 1/Study 1/s1_t2_anonymized.csv` for `Main_Analysis.R`; `Study 2/s2_t1_anonymized.csv` to `osfstorage-archive/Study 2/Study 2/s2_t1_anonymized.csv` for `Main_Analysis.R`. info.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion

text.text: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people's minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators.
Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information.
We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one's beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI).

To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294).
We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform.
In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility.

Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source.
These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility.
More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs.
Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.
Research shows that even a short conversation with AIs can change people's beliefs.

To better understand this persuasive ability, we examined how recipients' trust in AI and intellectual humility (acknowledging the limits of one's knowledge and openness to belief revision) jointly predict attitude change.
Among participants who initially opposed legal immigration, we replicated the finding that ChatGPT can shift attitudes.
Crucially, this shift was strongest among those who were both initially more open to belief revision and more trusting of the source.

Beyond AI persuasion, this suggests that source trust does not uniformly predict attitude change; its relationship with belief revision may depend on individuals' willingness to recognize the potential fallibility of their existing beliefs.
Beliefs are rarely revised in the face of factual, counter-attitudinal evidence (Kahan, 2013; Kunda, 1990).
text.formatted: Beliefs are rarely revised in the face of factual, counter-attitudinal evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kahan, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kunda, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: One prominent explanation for this resistance is motivated cognition, which biases how individuals engage with and interpret information in ways that align with prior beliefs and identities (Kunda, 1990).
text.formatted: One prominent explanation for this resistance is motivated cognition, which biases how individuals engage with and interpret information in ways that align with prior beliefs and identities <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kunda, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: This bias serves functional goals by reducing cognitive dissonance, maintaining social standing, and managing epistemic uncertainty, thereby offering an adaptive mechanism supporting coherent and socially embedded belief systems (Barlev & Neuberg, 2025; Kruglanski & Webster, 1996).
text.formatted: This bias serves functional goals by reducing cognitive dissonance, maintaining social standing, and managing epistemic uncertainty, thereby offering an adaptive mechanism supporting coherent and socially embedded belief systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barlev & Neuberg, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kruglanski & Webster, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this account of motivated cognition, recent evidence suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) may uniquely interact with these processes, both diminishing (Costello et al., 2024) and generating strongly held beliefs such as conspiracy theories (Costello et al., 2026), bypassing the skepticism and psychological resistance often triggered by human sources.
text.formatted: Building on this account of motivated cognition, recent evidence suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) may uniquely interact with these processes, both diminishing <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref> and generating strongly held beliefs such as conspiracy theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Costello et al., 2026)</ref>, bypassing the skepticism and psychological resistance often triggered by human sources.

text.text: This persuasive edge appears to stem, partially, from perceived objectivity and a lack of human fallibility (Sundar & Kim, 2019), resulting in trust levels that can exceed those of human counterparts (Boissin et al., 2025; Globig et al., 2025; von Sikorski et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This persuasive edge appears to stem, partially, from perceived objectivity and a lack of human fallibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Sundar & Kim, 2019)</ref>, resulting in trust levels that can exceed those of human counterparts <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Boissin et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Globig et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">von Sikorski et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, models like GPT-4foot_0 can appear more convincing than traditional information sources (Hackenburg et al., 2023 (Hackenburg et al., , 2025)), likely due to the fluency and ease of processing AI-generated text, a natural tone, high density of factual evidence, and people's preference for knowledge-based arguments over affective appeals (Watson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, models like GPT-4<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> can appear more convincing than traditional information sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hackenburg et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hackenburg et al., , 2025))</ref>, likely due to the fluency and ease of processing AI-generated text, a natural tone, high density of factual evidence, and people's preference for knowledge-based arguments over affective appeals <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Watson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, research has identified the central role of factual evidence in these interactions, without which persuasion is severely diminished (Costello et al., 2025; Hackenburg et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, research has identified the central role of factual evidence in these interactions, without which persuasion is severely diminished <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Costello et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hackenburg et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the interactive nature of LLMs enables a dynamic, conversational exchange in which the model adjusts its arguments in real-time and accounts for different claims, unlike static text (Costello et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, the interactive nature of LLMs enables a dynamic, conversational exchange in which the model adjusts its arguments in real-time and accounts for different claims, unlike static text <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Costello et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Combined with the ability to microtarget content based on individual traits (Simchon et al., 2023 (Simchon et al., , 2024)), LLMs' personalized arguments can outperform human debaters (Salvi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Combined with the ability to microtarget content based on individual traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Simchon et al., 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Simchon et al., , 2024))</ref>, LLMs' personalized arguments can outperform human debaters <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Salvi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Concerningly, this persuasive influence persists even when individuals are explicitly informed of the AI's intent and microtargeting tactics (Carrella et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Concerningly, this persuasive influence persists even when individuals are explicitly informed of the AI's intent and microtargeting tactics <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Carrella et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite AI's persuasive success across domains (Hornsey et al., 2026), it remains unclear whether these persuasive effects depend on the human recipient's characteristics.
text.formatted: Despite AI's persuasive success across domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hornsey et al., 2026)</ref>, it remains unclear whether these persuasive effects depend on the human recipient's characteristics.

text.text: We focus on two factors: trust in the information source and intellectual humility (IH).

Trust concerns the perceived reliability of the source, which can reduce defensive processing by increasing the likelihood that information is evaluated on its epistemic merits (Hornsey & Fielding, 2017; Pornpitakpan, 2004; Smith et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Trust concerns the perceived reliability of the source, which can reduce defensive processing by increasing the likelihood that information is evaluated on its epistemic merits <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hornsey & Fielding, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Pornpitakpan, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Smith et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: IH reflects acknowledgment of the limits of one's knowledge and openness to revising one's views (Porter et al., 2022).
text.formatted: IH reflects acknowledgment of the limits of one's knowledge and openness to revising one's views <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Porter et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The importance of source credibility has long been recognized within the persuasion literature.
Yet source credibility is ultimately consequential insofar as it translates into trust on the part of the recipient.

Dual-process models of persuasion, such as the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), propose that persuasive information can be processed either through systematic evaluation of the arguments themselves or through reliance on peripheral cues like the communicator's perceived trustworthiness, expertise, reputation, likeability (Pornpitakpan, 2004), and perceived consensus surrounding the claim (Chaiken, 1980; Metzger et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Dual-process models of persuasion, such as the Elaboration Likelihood Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)</ref>, propose that persuasive information can be processed either through systematic evaluation of the arguments themselves or through reliance on peripheral cues like the communicator's perceived trustworthiness, expertise, reputation, likeability <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Pornpitakpan, 2004)</ref>, and perceived consensus surrounding the claim <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chaiken, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Metzger et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Such cues allow individuals to accept or reject claims without deeply engaging with their content (Chaiken, 1980), particularly when evaluating argument quality is cognitively demanding or when individuals lack sufficient background knowledge.
text.formatted: Such cues allow individuals to accept or reject claims without deeply engaging with their content <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chaiken, 1980)</ref>, particularly when evaluating argument quality is cognitively demanding or when individuals lack sufficient background knowledge.

text.text: As a result, persuasion may depend on communicator characteristics (Hovland & Weiss, 1951), as well as the trust that emerges during the persuasive interaction, highlighting the influential role of credibility-related signals in shaping belief revision.
text.formatted: As a result, persuasion may depend on communicator characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hovland & Weiss, 1951)</ref>, as well as the trust that emerges during the persuasive interaction, highlighting the influential role of credibility-related signals in shaping belief revision.

text.text: Previous research on AI persuasion highlighted the role of trust in conversations with AI agents and LLMs, with Costello et al. (2024) finding that trust in AI and institutional trust moderated the effects of the intervention.
text.formatted: Previous research on AI persuasion highlighted the role of trust in conversations with AI agents and LLMs, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Costello et al. (2024)</ref> finding that trust in AI and institutional trust moderated the effects of the intervention.

text.text: Building on this work, we ask whether the relationship between preexisting source trust and attitude change depends on recipients' epistemic dispositions.

One epistemic disposition that may be particularly relevant in this context is intellectual humility (IH), which has been linked to overcoming biases in information processing, with converging evidence suggesting it is associated with more accurate epistemic functioning as well as with interactions with AIs (Costello et al., 2025).
text.formatted: One epistemic disposition that may be particularly relevant in this context is intellectual humility (IH), which has been linked to overcoming biases in information processing, with converging evidence suggesting it is associated with more accurate epistemic functioning as well as with interactions with AIs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Costello et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals higher in IH show greater metacognitive awareness and reduced susceptibility to misinformation (Prike et al., 2024), better discernment between facts and "alternative facts" (Newman et al., 2022), greater cognitive flexibility (Zmigrod et al., 2019), and increased attention to claims' evidentiary basis (Hoyle et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Individuals higher in IH show greater metacognitive awareness and reduced susceptibility to misinformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Prike et al., 2024)</ref>, better discernment between facts and "alternative facts" <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Newman et al., 2022)</ref>, greater cognitive flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Zmigrod et al., 2019)</ref>, and increased attention to claims' evidentiary basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hoyle et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: IH is also associated with greater openness to opposing political views (Porter & Schumann, 2018), more emotional and cognitive trust in others (Krumrei-Mancuso & Newman, 2020), and reduced confirmation and myside biases (Bowes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: IH is also associated with greater openness to opposing political views <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Porter & Schumann, 2018)</ref>, more emotional and cognitive trust in others (Krumrei-Mancuso & Newman, 2020), and reduced confirmation and myside biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bowes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, IH has a metacognitive component concerning the limits and potential fallibility of one's own knowledge, which can guide evidence-based inquiry (Ballantyne, 2023; Porter et al., 2025; Schwarz, 2023).
text.formatted: Crucially, IH has a metacognitive component concerning the limits and potential fallibility of one's own knowledge, which can guide evidence-based inquiry <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ballantyne, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Porter et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Schwarz, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although closely related to actively open-minded thinking, IH places a particular emphasis on one's epistemic stance toward one's own beliefs, whereas actively open-minded thinking emphasizes the tendency to consider alternative evidence and viewpoints during information processing (Newton et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although closely related to actively open-minded thinking, IH places a particular emphasis on one's epistemic stance toward one's own beliefs, whereas actively open-minded thinking emphasizes the tendency to consider alternative evidence and viewpoints during information processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Newton et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this metacognitive orientation, intellectually humble individuals more actively investigate evidence, including information that may confirm or challenge their existing views (Koetke et al., 2023), and are more willing to seek counter-attitudinal information (Koetke et al., 2022; Porter et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with this metacognitive orientation, intellectually humble individuals more actively investigate evidence, including information that may confirm or challenge their existing views <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Koetke et al., 2023)</ref>, and are more willing to seek counter-attitudinal information <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Koetke et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Porter et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is particularly relevant to belief revision, as considering alternative information is not equivalent to recognizing that one's own existing belief may be mistaken and require updating.

We therefore focus on intellectual humility as a disposition that may facilitate such recognition, while proposing that whether this openness translates into attitude change should depend on the perceived trustworthiness of the source providing the counter-attitudinal information.

We propose that intellectual humility provides the internal readiness to engage with counter-attitudinal evidence, whereas trust in the source determines whether such evidence is perceived as epistemically credible.
Accordingly, a metacognitive awareness of the limits of one's knowledge and openness to belief revision should lead to attitude change primarily when the source is perceived as trustworthy.

Conversely, trust in the source may not be sufficient when intellectual humility is low, because individuals unaware of the fallibility of their beliefs may be less willing to revise them, even when counter-attitudinal information comes from a trusted source.

Thus, we propose that intellectual humility and source trust play distinct but complementary roles, with attitude updating being most likely when individuals are both open to the possibility that their existing beliefs may be mistaken and willing to regard the source of corrective information as credible.

This perspective extends beyond AImediated persuasion; although source credibility can serve as a heuristic cue that promotes persuasion without extensive processing of message content (Chaiken, 1980; Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), we propose that its relationship with attitude change may also depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the potential fallibility of their existing beliefs.
text.formatted: This perspective extends beyond AImediated persuasion; although source credibility can serve as a heuristic cue that promotes persuasion without extensive processing of message content <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Chaiken, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)</ref>, we propose that its relationship with attitude change may also depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the potential fallibility of their existing beliefs.

text.text: This work advances our understanding of AI persuasion in several critical ways.

First, we assess trust in AI systems using a multidimensional framework assessing familiarity, perceived intentions, reliability, and distinct valences of trust and distrust (Jian et al., 2000), rather than relying on single items, allowing us to examine the role of source trust beyond a global evaluation of AI.
text.formatted: First, we assess trust in AI systems using a multidimensional framework assessing familiarity, perceived intentions, reliability, and distinct valences of trust and distrust <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Jian et al., 2000)</ref>, rather than relying on single items, allowing us to examine the role of source trust beyond a global evaluation of AI.

text.text: Importantly, measuring these trust dimensions before the interaction with the LLM in both studies, and using them as criteria for inclusion in the second part of the study, allowed us to further examine the role of preexisting trust in subsequent attitude updating.

Second, we introduce intellectual humility as a distinct epistemic trait, moving beyond general openness to specifically evaluate a person's willingness to recognize personal fallibility and revise beliefs in the face of counter-evidence, and we measured it before the interaction with the AI in Study 2.

Finally, and most importantly, we examine the joint role of these two preexisting dispositions; rather than asking only whether trust or epistemic openness predicts attitude change, we test whether openness to revising one's beliefs depends on regarding the source as credible, and whether trust in the source is sufficient in the absence of such openness.

This allows us to examine the theoretically proposed interplay between intellectual humility and source trust in predicting subsequent attitude updating in response to counter-attitudinal information, and to consider whether the relationship between source trust and attitude change depends on recipients' epistemic openness.
We applied Costello et al.'s (2024) GPT conversation paradigm in the context of a broad negative attitude.
text.formatted: We applied <ref type="bibr">Costello et al.'s (2024)</ref> GPT conversation paradigm in the context of a broad negative attitude.

text.text: Given the ethical sensitivity of persuasion designs, we focused on participants who held negative views of legal immigration, a central and contemporary issue that is likely to become increasingly relevant in global societies.

Unlike the effects of illegal immigration, which are harder to identify due to limited documentation, legal immigration is well documented, and there is factual evidence demonstrating its positive influence on recipient societies (e.g., Migration Advisory Committee, 2025).
In the analyses, we focused on the reported attitude after the conversation with GPT (T2) while holding the initial opinion (T1) constant, as was conducted in similar studies.

We hypothesized that, following a conversation with GPT, participants' opinion of legal immigrants would become more positive, particularly among those who exhibit higher trust in GPT and greater intellectual humility.
To measure participants' attitudes toward legal immigrants before the conversation with GPT, we recruited a sample of monolingual English speakers from the UK on Prolific.

Participants reported their opinion about legal immigrants and completed a general trust (Cronbach's α = .92) and distrust (Cronbach's α = .92) questionnaires toward GPT, adapted from Jian et al. (2000), all measured on 7-point Likert scales.
text.formatted: Participants reported their opinion about legal immigrants and completed a general trust (Cronbach's α = .92) and distrust (Cronbach's α = .92) questionnaires toward GPT, adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Jian et al. (2000)</ref>, all measured on 7-point Likert scales.

text.text: We prescreened participants so that only those with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants and who scored above the median on trust and below the median on distrust in GPT, or vice-versa, were invited to complete the main survey one week later (T2).
In it, participants were instructed to have a conversation with GPT-o1-mini, OpenAI's conversational chatbot.
The conversation began with the participants' response to the question: "In England, there is a population of legal immigrants.
What do you think about this issue?"
This response was sent to GPT's API, which generated replies across four conversational exchanges.

There was no manipulation or assignment to conditions, with the prompts being identical for all participants and variation in the conversations arising from participants' responses and the GPT-generated replies to those responses.
After the conversation, participants were asked how convincing and pleasant they found the exchange, using a 1-7 Likert scale.
They were then asked to list three to five statements that GPT had provided during the conversation, regardless of how much they agreed with them.
Participants rated the veracity of each statement and the extent to which the information was new to them.

Participants next completed the same trust and distrust questionnaires used in the pre-screening phase, presented in a counterbalanced order, as well as an interpersonal trust scale (Yamagishi, 1988; Cronbach's α = .86) and an intellectual humility scale (Leary et al., 2017;  Cronbach's α = .88).
text.formatted: Participants next completed the same trust and distrust questionnaires used in the pre-screening phase, presented in a counterbalanced order, as well as an interpersonal trust scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Yamagishi, 1988</ref>; Cronbach's α = .86) and an intellectual humility scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Leary et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> Cronbach's α = .88).

text.text: We also asked about the frequency and purposes of participants' use of GPT, and measured their attitude toward legal immigrants again.
Lastly, participants answered several demographic questions and were debriefed.
Preregistration: All studies received IRB approval and were preregistered prior to data collection (As predicted #208612).

text.text: As preregistered, we aimed to recruit 200 participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants.
To this end, we invited 1,302 monolingual English speakers from the UK to report their opinion about legal immigrants (T1).
Of these, 258 participants held a negative attitude, as reflected by a score below 4 on a 7-point Likert scale.

There was no significant difference in initial trust in GPT between those with a positive (M = 4.05, SD = 1.26) compared to a negative (M = 4.01, SD = 1.39) opinion about legal immigrants (p = .650) nor in distrust (M pro immigrants = 3.34, SD = 1.38, M anti immigrants = 3.46, SD = 1.42, p = .248).
In addition to a negative attitude toward immigrants, we sought to ensure sufficient variance in participants' trust (Median = 4.17) and distrust (Median = 3.20) in GPT.

Thus, only those who were above the median in trust and below the median in distrust (n = 91), and the inverse group, those above the median in distrust and below the median in trust (n = 100), were invited to the main survey.
A total of 124 participants completed the main study (T2).

As preregistered, we excluded three participants who experienced a disturbance or a technical problem during the study, three who did not complete the survey consecutively, one who admitted to careless responding, and two additional participants who took longer than 3 SD above the mean completion time (M completion time = 17.49 minutes, SD = 8.58 minutes).

Due to technical issues, we did not have complete responses for three additional participants, and seven additional participants could not be matched with responses in T1, resulting in 105 participants (M age = 42.94), of whom 58 (55%) identified as male, 46 (43.8%) as female, and one as "other".

The mean opinion about legal immigrants at the first measurement was 2.23 (SD = 0.79), but after the conversation with GPT, it significantly increased to 3.82 (SD = 1.84), t(104) = -8.89, p < .001 (Figure 1).

found that the attitudes toward legal immigrants at T1 were a significant positive predictor of the attitudes at T2 (b = .50, SE = 0.22, t = 2.34, p = .02), suggesting that this attitude is generally stable.

Trust in GPT at T1 was a significant negative predictor (b = -1.22, SE = 0.57, t = -2.15, p = .034), indicating that higher initial trust in GPT was associated with less positive attitudes toward immigrants after the conversation with GPT while holding intellectual humility at zero.
Intellectual humility at T2 was not a significant predictor (p = .30) when trust was at zero.

Crucially, there was a significant interaction between trust at T1 and intellectual humility at T2 (b = .35, SE = 0.14, t = 2.42, p = .017), such that participants who were both higher in trust and higher in intellectual humility expressed more positive opinions of legal immigrants after exposure to counter-attitudinal claims, while holding constant their initial attitude toward legal immigrants (Figure 2).

text.text: A simple slope analysis showed that at mean levels of trust, intellectual humility significantly predicted more positive attitudes at T2 (b = .8, SE = 0.27, p = .004).

We found that following a conversation with GPT presenting counter-attitudinal factual information, participants' attitudes toward legal immigrants became more positive, replicating existing findings on the effectiveness of AI persuasion (Costello et al., 2024; Hornsey et al., 2026).

text.text: We focused on two crucial components in AI-mediated persuasion: trust in the source -measured before the conversation with GPT, and IH.
For intellectually humble individuals, low trust may limit persuasion because there is no credible channel from which to accept new information.

Conversely, source credibility alone cannot overcome rigid beliefs; without openness to counter-attitudinal information, even a trusted source presenting confrontational evidence may be dismissed or discredited.
However, IH was measured only after the conversation with GPT, limiting the directionality of the association.

Although higher IH was related to greater attitude change, we cannot determine whether IH preceded openness to counter-attitudinal information or whether exposure to such information and the experience of changing one's mind was associated with higher self-reported humility.
To clarify this relationship, Study 2 measured IH and trust in GPT before the AI-conversation.

Method Study 2 replicated the design of Study 1 with two main modifications aimed at clarifying the directional relationship between intellectual humility and opinion change following exposure to counter-attitudinal information, as well as testing the durability of such changes.
The first modification was the addition of a baseline measure of intellectual humility (Leary et al., 2017; Cronbach's α = .86) during the prescreening stage (T1).
text.formatted: The first modification was the addition of a baseline measure of intellectual humility <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Leary et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cronbach'</ref>s α = .86) during the prescreening stage (T1).

text.text: The intellectual humility scale was adapted to a 7-point response format to align with the additional measures of trust (α = .92) and distrust (α = .91) in ChatGPT.

The second modification was the inclusion of a follow-up measurement one week after the conversation (T3), which assessed attitudes toward legal immigrants, intellectual humility, trust, and distrust.

This design allowed us to test whether intellectual humility at T1 predicts opinion change following an interaction with GPT, whether opinion change at T2 predicts increased intellectual humility at T3, or both, and whether attitude change persists over time.

The procedure at T2 was identical to Study 1, wherein participants engaged in four exchanges with GPT based on the same prompts and instructions, with the exception that the trust and distrust questionnaires were omitted at T2.

Measurements of intellectual humility at T1 and interpersonal trust at T2 (α = .82) allowed us to distinguish between associations linking initial intellectual humility with the acceptance of counter-attitudinal information and associations linking such exposure with subsequent intellectual humility.
All hypotheses and methods were preregistered prior to data collection (As Predicted #218144).
The analysis plan was preregistered, but there were deviations from the preregistration due to participant attrition.

text.text: We aimed to recruit 200 participants for the T3 follow-up and therefore sampled participants in three waves over the course of one month.
In total, 1,448 participants completed the prescreening protocol (T1).
Invitations to participate in T2 were restricted to participants who expressed negative attitudes toward legal immigrants at T1 (scores < 4), yielding 540 eligible participants.
text.formatted: Invitations to participate in T2 were restricted to participants who expressed negative attitudes toward legal immigrants at T1 (scores < 4), yielding 540 eligible participants.

text.text: Of these, only participants who scored above the median in trust in GPT and below the median in distrust in GPT (n = 177), as well as the inverse group, those above the median in distrust and below the median in trust in GPT (n = 213), were invited to participate in T2 (n = 390 participants).
Of the 390 eligible participants, 213 completed T2, of whom 211 could be matched to their T1 data (54.1% of the eligible sample).
Participants who did not return to complete T2 did not differ significantly in their mean scores of trust and IH, nor did attrition rates differ significantly between the high-and low-trust groups.
Full analyses are available in the supplementary materials.
Following preregistered exclusion criteria, eight participants were excluded due to technical issues, and seven additional participants did not complete the survey consecutively.
Four participants indicated that their data should not be used, and three participants took more than 3 SD above the mean completion time (M completion time = 16.17 minutes, SD = 6.54 minutes).
Two additional participants were excluded because they provided an ID that did not match the first wave for a total of 189 participants.
The mean age of the sample was 41.89 years (SD = 11.58), 52.9% of participants identified as male, 46.6% identified as female, and one participant identified as "other".
One week later, of the participants invited back for T3, 152 provided data utilized in our longitudinal structural equation model.

At baseline, participants with positive attitudes toward legal immigrants reported higher trust in GPT (M = 4.35, SD = 1.26) compared to those with negative attitudes (M = 4.15, SD = 1.39), t(1047.5) = 2.72, p = .007, 95% CI [0.06, 0.34], d = 0.15.
There were no significant differences in distrust (p = .10).

Participants with positive attitudes were, however, more intellectually humble (M = 5.37, SD = 0.87) than those with negative attitudes (M = 5.11, SD = 0.99), t(1446) = 5.15, p < .001, 95% CI [0.16, 0.35], d = 0.28.

text.text: We preregistered a linear regression model predicting attitudes toward legal immigrants at T2 from baseline attitudes (T1), intellectual humility (T1), trust in GPT (T1), and their interaction.
Baseline attitudes significantly predicted subsequent attitudes (b = 0.52, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [0.23, 0.81], p < .001).

text.text: When examining the main effects, intellectual humility (b = -0.21, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.39], p = .49) and trust in GPT (b = -0.45, SE = 0.35, 95% CI [-1.13, 0.24], p = .20) were not significant predictors individually.

The preregistered interaction between intellectual humility and trust in GPT was in the same direction as observed in Study 1 but was not significant (b = 0.11, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.25], p = .09), likely reflecting insufficient statistical power.

Examining the simple slopes for participants with high levels (+1SD from the mean) of trust, there was a positive and significant relationship between intellectual humility and attitude change (b = 0.45, SE = 0.15, p = .004).

In contrast, for those with low levels of trust (-1SD from the mean), this relationship disappeared (b = 0.10, SE = 0.15, p = .52), suggesting that even when a participant is intellectually humble, they do not change their attitudes if they do not trust the source, emphasizing the centrality of both factors.

To address the power limitations of the preregistered regression and to maximize the available information, we employed a structural equation modeling (SEM) approach using full information maximum likelihood (FIML).
This approach enabled us to model stability paths across time and to estimate the preregistered interaction using all available data (n = 390).
The initial SEM demonstrated poor fit, χ²(11) = 48.069, p < .001, χ²/df = 4.37, CFI = .979, TLI = .947, RMSEA = .093, 90% CI [.067, .121], SRMR = .052.

The model revealed clear differences across the three time points.

In Study 2, we measured both trust in AI and intellectual humility before the conversation with GPT.
This temporal ordering allowed us to examine whether preexisting differences in these constructs predicted subsequent attitude change and, critically, whether their effects depended on one another.
We found that the interaction between IH and trust in the source predicted subsequent attitude change, over and above their individual associations with attitude change.
Specifically, greater trust was associated with more favorable attitude change only among participants higher in IH.

The third measurement further showed that the more favorable attitudes toward legal immigrants observed after the conversation remained elevated one week later, providing evidence that the attitude change was not limited to the immediate aftermath of the interaction.
Across two studies, we found that initial trust in the source and intellectual humility interact to predict acceptance of counter-attitudinal information from AI.
Our findings replicate and elaborate AI-persuasion research by examining how the relationship between preexisting source trust and attitude change depends on recipients' intellectual humility.

We find that the interplay between IH and preexisting trust is important: when openness to changing one's mind is low, counter-attitudinal, identity-challenging information may be met with resistance despite trust in the source.
When trust in the source is low, counter-attitudinal information may be overlooked and evaluated as untrustworthy, despite a general openness.
Hence, our findings limit the persuasive potential of AI by identifying an important boundary condition: the interaction between recipients' intellectual humility and their initial trust in AI.
These findings illuminate a new aspect of classical persuasion models, like the Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), by reframing the role of source credibility.
text.formatted: These findings illuminate a new aspect of classical persuasion models, like the Elaboration Likelihood Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)</ref>, by reframing the role of source credibility.

text.text: Within the context of strongly entrenched beliefs, we suggest that source trustworthiness may constitute a meaningful factor that individuals actively attend to, rather than operating solely as a heuristic cue that facilitates persuasion independently of the recipient's epistemic disposition.
Our findings suggest that the extent to which source trustworthiness facilitates belief revision depends on the recipient's level of intellectual humility.

Among more intellectually humble individuals, greater trust in the source was associated with greater revision of prior attitudes, consistent with the possibility that trust facilitates openness to counter-attitudinal information when individuals are willing to recognize the limits of their own knowledge.

In contrast, for those lower in intellectual humility, greater trust did not produce the same pattern of attitude revision, suggesting that persuasion depends on the recipient's epistemic disposition.
Lower intellectual humility may limit individuals' willingness to reconsider their existing beliefs, even when the information comes from a trusted source.
Conversely, greater intellectual humility may facilitate receptivity to counter-attitudinal information when the source is perceived as trustworthy.

Our findings thus suggest that source trust may play a role beyond serving as a heuristic cue: its relationship with attitude change appears to depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the potential fallibility of their existing beliefs.
This positions the interaction between trust and IH as a key theoretical boundary condition in understanding when source credibility is associated with belief revision.
Future research could extend these insights in at least two directions.
First, testing whether similar effects would emerge in human-to-human exchanges.

Second, within human-AI interactions, future research could address a paradoxical risk -while IH may support evidence-based belief updating, it does not account for misplaced trust, which can induce unfounded beliefs (Costello et al., 2026) and amplify biases embedded in training data (Glickman & Sharot, 2025).
text.formatted: Second, within human-AI interactions, future research could address a paradoxical risk -while IH may support evidence-based belief updating, it does not account for misplaced trust, which can induce unfounded beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Costello et al., 2026)</ref> and amplify biases embedded in training data <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Glickman & Sharot, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, sycophantic and pleasing features of AI responses in the context of persuasion are uncommon among human communicators in the same setting and could be confused for cues of trustworthiness.
Such responses can facilitate attitude change when the AIs are providing a contradicting perspective, but they can also sustain misguided beliefs and curtail critical thinking (Rathje et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such responses can facilitate attitude change when the AIs are providing a contradicting perspective, but they can also sustain misguided beliefs and curtail critical thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Rathje et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The possibility of misinterpreting cues of credibility is compounded by findings suggesting that AI guardrails may be weaker than we thought (Kowal et al., 2025), that models do not default to factuality unless explicitly prompted (Hackenburg et al., 2025), and evidence suggesting that humans have a limited ability to identify (Spitale et al., 2023) hallucinations or deceptive outputs generated by GPT and other LLMs (Klingbeil et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The possibility of misinterpreting cues of credibility is compounded by findings suggesting that AI guardrails may be weaker than we thought <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kowal et al., 2025)</ref>, that models do not default to factuality unless explicitly prompted <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hackenburg et al., 2025)</ref>, and evidence suggesting that humans have a limited ability to identify <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Spitale et al., 2023)</ref> hallucinations or deceptive outputs generated by GPT and other LLMs <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Klingbeil et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, considering the growing dependence on AIs, we suggest that their persuasive impact may be bound by the dispositions of the human receivers, specifically pre-existing trust and intellectual humility.

Our findings suggest that IH may contribute to receptivity to counter-attitudinal information rather than necessarily implying indiscriminate openness, with source trust playing a complementary role in determining when such openness is associated with attitude change.

Results indicated strong autoregressive stability for attitudes and intellectual humility across time.
Attitudes at T2 were strongly predicted by baseline attitudes (b = 0.52, SE = 0.15, 95% CI [0.24, 0.81], p < .001).

text.text: Regarding the predictors of interest, intellectual humility at T1 did not predict attitudes at T2 when trust was at zero (b = -0.34, SE = 0.28, 95% CI [-0.89, 0.21], p = .22).

Trust in GPT at T1 negatively predicted attitudes at T2 when intellectual humility was at zero (b = -0.65, SE = 0.31, 95% CI [-1.26, -0.04], p = .038), but not at mean levels of intellectual humility (b = 0.09, SE = 0.07, p = .22).

Importantly, the preregistered interaction between intellectual humility and trust in GPT at T1 significantly predicted attitudes at T2 (b = 0.14, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.03, 0.26], p = .016), consistent with the pattern observed in Study 1.
This interaction suggests that the association between trust in GPT and subsequent attitudes became more positive as intellectual humility increased.

Over time, attitudes at T2 strongly predicted attitudes at T3 (b = 0.64, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.53, 0.75], p < .001), while intellectual humility at T2 did not predict later attitudes (b = 0.04, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.20], p = .57).

text.text: By the later follow-up (T3), attitudes showed a significant decline compared to T2 with a mean score of 3.06 (SD = 1.62) (b = 0.54, SE = 0.11, 95% CI [0.28, 0.81], p < .001), reflecting partial attenuation of the initial boost.
text.formatted: By the later follow-up (T3), attitudes showed a significant decline compared to T2 with a mean score of 3.06 (SD = 1.62) (b = 0.54, SE = 0.11, 95% CI [0.28, 0.81], p < .001), reflecting partial attenuation of the initial boost.

text.text: Importantly, however, attitudes at T3 remained significantly higher than at baseline (b = -0.93, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [-1.17, -0.68], p < .001), demonstrating that the intervention produced a lasting positive shift over time despite some reduction from the immediate post-intervention peak.
